name: Benelli (donut) mastopexy

card.summary: A breast lift that removes a ring of skin around the areola and closes it with a purse-string suture, raising the nipple and reshaping a mildly to moderately sagging breast with a single circular scar.
card.aka: donut lift, round block mastopexy, circumareolar mastopexy
card.note: Surgical procedure with a circular scar; smoking and other factors are linked to higher nipple-necrosis risk.

quick.overview:
The Benelli or donut mastopexy is a breast-lift operation. A doughnut-shaped ring of skin around the areola is removed and the outer skin is gathered in toward the areola with a deep permanent stitch. The result is a higher nipple position and a tighter, more lifted breast contour, with the scar hidden at the edge of the areola.

It is described in surgical references as suited to mild to moderate sagging (ptosis), and it is also used in oncoplastic breast-conserving surgery and for tubular breast shapes. Published case reports and technique papers describe its use for both cosmetic and reconstructive aims.
quick.how: It is performed by a plastic surgeon under anesthesia. The circular skin pattern is marked around the areola, the ring of skin is removed, the breast tissue may be reshaped, and a purse-string suture secures the new areola size. It is sometimes combined with an implant. Healing and scar maturation continue for months.
quick.risks: Surgical references list bleeding, infection, numbness, asymmetry, wound separation and nipple or skin necrosis as possible complications. Smoking, diabetes, obesity and aspirin use are associated with higher necrosis risk. Critics of periareolar patterns describe a flattened or bottom-heavy shape and a widened or puckered scar in some patients; the areola can also stretch over time.

lead: The Benelli mastopexy, also called the donut lift or round block technique, is a breast-lift procedure in which a ring of skin around the areola is removed and the remaining skin is gathered toward the areola with a purse-string suture [1][3]. It lifts the nipple-areola complex and tightens the breast envelope, giving a higher, firmer-looking breast, and it leaves one circular scar at the areola border rather than the vertical or fold scars of other lifts [1].

It is named for the Italian surgeon Louis Benelli, whose round block technique was published in the early 1990s; a 1993 paper described a modified purse-string version for true ptosis and tubular breast deformity [2]. Surgeons also use the same method in oncoplastic breast-conserving surgery, where it displaces volume to fill the space left after tumor removal [4].

Within looksmaxxing and body-aesthetics discussion it appears as one of the lift options within hardmaxxing (surgical) approaches to breast shape. Published literature consists of surgical technique papers and case series rather than controlled trials.

angle.text: The procedure repositions the nipple and breast skin upward, changing the profile of a mildly to moderately sagging breast. People choose it when they want a lift with the shortest scar pattern.

paras: In the Benelli technique, the surgeon marks two concentric circles around the areola and removes the skin between them. The outer skin is then brought in toward the areola and secured with a permanent purse-string suture, which is intended to hold the areola at its new diameter [1][3]. Wikipedia's mastopexy article describes it as the circumareolar or donut lift, in which the only scar is circular, and notes that a permanent deep suture is typically used to prevent the areola from widening [3].

Mastopexy techniques are generally grouped by scar pattern: anchor (inverted-T), lollipop (circumvertical), crescent, and circumareolar. The article lists the donut lift as a choice for moderate ptosis, with the anchor pattern reserved for severe ptosis [3].

People seeking a lift after pregnancy, weight loss or menopause may consider it when sagging is mild to moderate and they prefer limited scarring [3]. A modified round block approach has been described for true ptosis, tubular breast deformity and its lesser forms [2].

The round block technique is used as a volume-displacement method in breast-conserving surgery for benign multicentric fibroadenomas and early cancers; a Nepalese case series followed four patients treated this way [4].

General surgical risks include bleeding, infection and anesthesia effects. Specific risks named in the literature are skin or nipple necrosis, numbness or tingling, seroma, hematoma, wound separation, asymmetry and contour irregularity. Smoking, diabetes, obesity and aspirin use are associated with higher nipple-necrosis risk, and combining a lift with augmentation raises complication rates [3].
Periareolar results are described by some sources as potentially bottom-heavy, with puckered or widened scars; scars fade but remain visible [3].

Published evidence consists mainly of technique descriptions and case series. A 1993 paper in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery described a modified round block mastopexy for true breast ptosis and tubular breast deformity and set out the anatomic reasoning for it [2]. A 2019 Kathmandu University Medical Journal report followed four patients treated with the original round block technique in breast-conserving surgery [4]. No randomized controlled trials were found.
